system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 14 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2146-05-11 20:21:00 to 2146-05-25 17:38:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of polymyositis, morbid obesity, recurrent pulmonary emboli, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and a 40-pound weight gain over one month. Initial concern for pulmonary embolism was raised due to subtherapeutic INR of 1.5, but CT angiography ruled out central PE, though image quality limited exclusion of peripheral clots. She was bridged with heparin and restarted on warfarin, reaching a therapeutic INR of 2.3 by discharge. Her symptoms were attributed to acute on chronic diastolic heart failure exacerbated by fluid retention, likely related to steroid use. She received IV furosemide with improvement in symptoms and weight reduction to 425 lbs, her baseline. Her home furosemide was increased to twice daily, and metoprolol was slightly increased, though limited by blood pressure. Polymyositis remained stable, with elevated but stable CK and downtrending troponin. She was discharged with instructions to monitor weight, avoid high-salt foods, check BMP in one week, and follow up with her primary care and cardiology providers.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic heart failure
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

Patient is a ___ female with PMHx polymyositis, sleep disordered

#. Cough, dyspnea and hypoxia: The etiology of her dyspnea and

CPAP and oxygen at night. By the time of discharge, patient was 
only requiring oxygen at night. She will have PFTs as an 
outpatient and has close follow-up with pulmonary. 
  
#. Polymyositis: Patient was admitted and complained of 
increasing weakness. Her CKs were elevated and continued to rise 
throughout her stay. She was initially treated with high dose 
methylprednisone iv but was then transitioned back to her home 
regimen until infection etiology could be ruled out. She was 
then started on methylprednisolone 20 mg iv BID and was given an 
infusion of rituximab on ___. She was discharged on 
methylprednisone 20 mg po daily with plan for repeat rituxmab 
infusion on ___ and rheum follow up on ___.  
 
#. Chest pain: Resolved by the time she was she was admitted to 
the medicine florr. Her ECG was not suggestive of ischemia and 
her troponins trended down. She was initially monitored on 
telemetry and  may have been related to underlying lung disease. 
Troponins trended down and she had no further episodes of chest 
pressure. 

#. History of DVT/PE: Patient was admitted with a subtherapeutic 
INR. She was intermittently on a heparin drip. She had 
hemoptysis after her bronchoscopy and her heparin and coumadin 
were held briefly as risk of bleeding from biopsy sites 
outweighed risk of repeat PE/ DVT (last ___ ___. She was then 
restarted on warfarin 10 mg daily and will follow up with the 
___ clinic. 

#. Tachycardia:  Chronic issue, may be worsened by hypoxia, 
appears to be improving. She was continued on her home 
metoprolol. Her TSH was normal.   

#. Microcytic Anemia: Stable, at baseline. Iron studies were 
suggestive of iron deficiency anemia. Iron 21, ferritin 51. She 
was started on iron replacement and her hematocrit improved. 
   
#. Chronic dCHF: Patient's BNP was elevated but not 
significantly elevated to suggest pulmonary edema but may still 
be contributing to dyspnea. She was continued on her home lasix. 

  
#. Diabetes: Her fingersticks stable on humalog insulin sliding 
scale (all <200) over her admission. Here metformin was held 
throughout her admission and was restarted on discharge. 

#. Depression: Stable but patient was frustrated at times with 
her condition and symptoms. She was seen by social work multiple

She received IV furosemide with improvement in symptoms and weight reduction to 425 lbs, her baseline. Her home furosemide was increased to twice daily, and metoprolol was slightly increased, though limited by blood pressure. Polymyositis remained stable, with elevated but stable CK and downtrending troponin. She was discharged with instructions to monitor weight, avoid high-salt foods, check BMP in one week, and follow up with her primary care and cardiology providers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having a lot of trouble breathing. It’s gotten worse over the past few days. I couldn’t even walk across the room without stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned chest pressure too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it felt like an elephant was sitting on my chest. It happened at 3 a.m. and lasted about an hour and a half. Then again this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. We checked your ECG and troponin, and there’s no sign of a heart attack. The chest pressure may be related to your lung issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was really worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT scan of your chest. It shows no blood clots in your lungs, which is good. But there are changes in your lung tissue—worsening interstitial lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my polymyositis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It could be a flare of your polymyositis affecting your lungs, or another condition like pneumonia. We’re still working it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also had a cough with yellow sputum and a fever a couple days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your white blood cell count is elevated, so there might be an infection, but we’re not sure yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my oxygen more during the day because I’m so short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll keep you on oxygen and monitor your levels. We also noticed your INR was low—1.1—so you’re not protected against clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been taking my warfarin the last few days because I couldn’t get up to take my evening meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart it carefully. For now, we’re giving you IV heparin to bridge you until your INR is therapeutic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative, and the sputum test didn’t show any serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a typical one. We’re still concerned about your lung changes. Your rheumatologist thinks this could be a flare of your polymyositis affecting your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My muscles have been hurting more, especially in my thighs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your CK level is very high—over 3,000—which suggests muscle inflammation. We’re increasing your steroid dose to help control the flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 6 mg of Medrol. Is that changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on 20 mg daily. We’ll watch for side effects, but it’s important to get the inflammation under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is still labored. We’re considering a bronchoscopy to get a better look and sample from your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m a bit nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common procedure. We’ll use sedation, and a specialist will guide a small tube into your airways. The goal is to rule out infection or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bronchoscopy went well. We took samples from your lungs. No cancer cells were found, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gram stain showed some gram-negative rods and yeast, but the culture grew only normal mouth bacteria. It’s likely contamination, not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing my breathing problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We still think it’s mostly due to your polymyositis flare and interstitial lung disease. The steroids should help, and we’re adding a rituximab infusion to calm your immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had the rituximab infusion yesterday. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. My breathing isn’t as bad, and I can talk in longer sentences now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your oxygen needs have gone down. You’re now only using it at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it briefly after the bronchoscopy because of a small risk of bleeding. But now that you’re stable, we’ve restarted it at 10 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your white count is coming down, and your CK is starting to drop—now at 1,689.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My thigh pain is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the treatment is working. We also checked your iron—it’s low. So we’re starting you on iron pills to help with your anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling tired. I guess that explains it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing continues to improve. The crackles in your lungs are less noticeable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I even walked to the bathroom this morning with help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re planning to discharge you in a couple of days if this trend continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest chest X-ray shows less congestion. Your heart size is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my face—it’s been itchy and scaly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s a mild rash, possibly related to your steroids. We’re adding a low-strength steroid ointment for 10 days—desonide. Avoid the eyelids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. We’ll see if you can go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But I’m nervous about managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a nurse to help you. And you’ll follow up with your rheumatologist and pulmonologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. Your discharge summary is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the main diagnosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interstitial lung disease and a flare of your polymyositis. Your shortness of breath was due to these, not a heart issue or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 20 mg of Medrol daily, iron once a day, and Bactrim every day for pneumonia prevention. We’re also continuing your warfarin at 10 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the rituximab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get another infusion in two weeks. Your rheumatologist will schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep using it at night. We’ll check your levels again in pulmonary clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep monitoring your weight, take your meds, and call if you have trouble breathing again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. You’re alert, breathing well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to leave. A home health nurse will visit you. Follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of polymyositis, morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic pulmonary emboli was admitted for progressively severe shortness of breath, chest pressure, and a productive cough. Initial evaluation ruled out pulmonary embolism but revealed worsening interstitial lung disease. Her symptoms were attributed to a flare of polymyositis with lung involvement and possible respiratory infection, though extensive microbiologic testing did not confirm an active infection. She was treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, transitioned to oral steroids, and received a rituximab infusion. Her anticoagulation was managed with heparin bridging and warfarin restart after a bronchoscopy. Iron supplementation was initiated for iron deficiency anemia. By discharge, her respiratory status improved, oxygen requirements decreased to nighttime use, and she was able to ambulate with assistance. She was discharged on increased prednisone, daily Bactrim, iron, and warfarin, with plans for outpatient pulmonary function tests and rheumatology follow-up including a second rituximab infusion.
